---
title: "Email security"
subtitle: "Understand how email moves, which identities are being authenticated, and how to determine whether a message passes DMARC."
---

## How email works

::: {.light-content}
![Each hop adds a Received header. One server can perform several roles.](files/images/email-flow.png){fig-alt="Mail flow: author's MUA submits to an MSA, which relays to a sending MTA, which uses SMTP to the receiving MX, which delivers through an MDA to the recipient's MUA. DNS supplies MX and policy records."}
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![Each hop adds a Received header. One server can perform several roles.](files/images/email-flow-dark.png){fig-alt="Mail flow: author's MUA submits to an MSA, which relays to a sending MTA, which uses SMTP to the receiving MX, which delivers through an MDA to the recipient's MUA. DNS supplies MX and policy records."}
:::

The roles come from [RFC 5598](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5598.html), Internet Mail Architecture:

| Role | What it does | Typical protocol and port |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **MUA**, Mail User Agent | The author's or recipient's client: Outlook, a phone, a web client | Submission out, IMAP/POP/HTTPS in |
| **MSA**, Mail Submission Agent | Accepts new mail from users and applications, usually after they authenticate | SMTP submission: 587 (STARTTLS), 465 (implicit TLS), and sometimes 25 |
| **MTA**, Mail Transfer Agent | Relays between servers; the receiving one is the **MX** | SMTP, port 25 |
| **MDA**, Mail Delivery Agent | Puts the message in the mailbox | Local |

**An MSA does not have to require authentication, or use port 587.** [RFC 6409](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6409.html) §4.3 says an MSA must reject unauthenticated mail by default "unless it has already independently established authentication or authorization (such as being within a protected subnetwork)", and §3.1 says "A site MAY choose to use port 25 for message submission." That is how printers, scanners and line-of-business applications send: an unauthenticated relay on port 25 that trusts their IP addresses, such as an Exchange receive connector or a Microsoft 365 connector. It is also why an internal relay that accepts anything from the network is worth finding during an incident. Port 465 with TLS from the first byte is [RFC 8314](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8314.html).

A sending MTA finds where to deliver by looking up the recipient domain's **MX** records in DNS, then connects to port 25 on the lowest-preference host that answers. In Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, one service performs every role; the distinctions still show up in the headers.

## The envelope versus the message

SMTP ([RFC 5321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321.html)) carries a message ([RFC 5322](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5322.html)) the way an envelope carries a letter. They have separate addresses, and they do not have to agree.

In the transcripts on this page, [what the client sends]{.smtp-client} and [what the server answers]{.smtp-server} are colored differently, and [annotations]{.smtp-note} are gray.

```smtp
S: 220 mx1.example.net ESMTP
C: EHLO out-12.esp.example
S: 250-mx1.example.net
C: MAIL FROM:<bounce-7731@mailer.esp.example>      <- envelope sender (RFC5321.MailFrom)
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<pat@example.net>                         <- envelope recipient
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: From: "Example County IT" <it-alerts@example.org>   <- message author (RFC5322.From)
C: To: pat@example.net
C: Subject: Scheduled maintenance this weekend
C:
C: ...
C: .
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued
```

::: {.output-note}
Constructed transcript with reserved example names. Each client command gets a numbered reply from the server before the next one. The two `From` addresses are different on purpose: this is how every email service provider and mailing list works.
:::

- `MAIL FROM` and `RCPT TO` are SMTP commands, not message headers. `RCPT TO` is why Bcc works: the recipient is on the envelope, not in the message.
- **`From`** is the author. It is what the user sees, and it is what DMARC protects.
- **`Sender`** names who actually sent the message on the author's behalf, when that differs (RFC 5322 §3.6.2). Outlook shows it as "*Sender* on behalf of *From*".
- **`Return-Path`** is added by the final delivering server, recording the `MAIL FROM` address (RFC 5321 §4.4). Bounces go there.
- **`Reply-To`** is where replies go. A mismatched `Reply-To` is common in business email compromise.

## Reading email headers

Download the [constructed sample message](files/samples/email/constructed-headers.eml) to follow along. It uses reserved names (RFC 2606) and documentation addresses (RFC 5737).

**Use Microsoft's Message Header Analyzer.** Paste headers into the [web version](https://mha.azurewebsites.net/pages/mha.html), or install the [Outlook add-in](https://appsource.microsoft.com/en-us/product/office/WA104005406), and it lays out the hops with the delay at each one, the authentication results, and the anti-spam headers Microsoft 365 adds. The add-in needs mailbox permissions, so an administrator usually deploys it. Reading the raw headers yourself, as below, is still worth practicing: it is what you do when a tool's interpretation looks wrong.

```text
Return-Path: <bounce-7731@mailer.esp.example>
Received: from mx1.example.net (mx1.example.net [198.51.100.25])
	by mbox1.example.net (Postfix) with ESMTPS id 4F2A11C0042
	for <pat@example.net>; Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:02:11 -0500 (CDT)
Authentication-Results: mx1.example.net;
	spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=mailer.esp.example;
	dkim=pass header.d=example.org header.s=esp2026 header.b=Qx3fK9aL;
	dmarc=pass header.from=example.org
Received: from out-12.esp.example (out-12.esp.example [203.0.113.40])
	by mx1.example.net (Postfix) with ESMTPS id 9C77E2A0011
	for <pat@example.net>; Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:02:10 -0500 (CDT)
Authentication-Results: out-12.esp.example; dkim=pass header.d=example.org; dmarc=pass
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=example.org;
	s=esp2026; t=1792177329; h=from:to:subject:date:message-id;
	bh=47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=;
	b=Qx3fK9aL...
Received: from app01.example.org (app01.example.org [192.0.2.17])
	by out-12.esp.example (Postfix) with ESMTPSA id 0B1D4400A3
	for <pat@example.net>; Fri, 16 Oct 2026 19:02:09 +0000 (UTC)
From: "Example County IT" <it-alerts@example.org>
Reply-To: helpdesk@example.org
To: pat@example.net
Subject: Scheduled maintenance this weekend
Date: Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:02:08 -0500
Message-ID: <20261016190208.12345@app01.example.org>
```

### `Received` headers and the path a message took

Each server prepends a `Received` header, so the newest is at the top. Read from the bottom up:

1. `app01.example.org [192.0.2.17]` submitted to the provider `out-12.esp.example` with **ESMTPSA**: SMTP with TLS (S) and authentication (A).
2. `out-12.esp.example [203.0.113.40]` relayed to the recipient's MX, `mx1.example.net`. **This is the connection SPF evaluated**: 203.0.113.40 is the IP the receiver saw.
3. `mx1.example.net` handed it to the mailbox server.

Compare timestamps across hops (converting time zones) to find delays. The `from` name in a `Received` header is what the connecting host claimed in `EHLO`; the name and IP in parentheses are what the receiving server observed.

### `Authentication-Results` and which system added them

[RFC 8601](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8601) defines `Authentication-Results`. The first token is the **authserv-id**: the system that did the checking. This message has two. Only `mx1.example.net` is the recipient's own boundary; the one from `out-12.esp.example` was added by the sender's provider and proves nothing to the recipient.

| Result | Identity checked | Value here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spf=pass` | `smtp.mailfrom`, the envelope domain | `mailer.esp.example` |
| `dkim=pass` | `header.d`, the signing domain, with `header.s` the selector | `example.org`, selector `esp2026` |
| `dmarc=pass` | `header.from`, the author domain | `example.org` |

SPF passed for the provider's domain, which does not align with `example.org`. DMARC still passes, because DKIM passed **and** its `d=` matches the `From` domain.

### Which headers can be trusted?

Only those added by systems you control: everything at and above your own boundary MX's first `Received` header. Anything below it was written by the sender or by servers you do not operate, and can be forged, including `Received` and `Authentication-Results` headers. A well-behaved receiver removes `Authentication-Results` headers that claim its own authserv-id before adding its own.

Forwarding and mailing lists break SPF (a new IP) and often DKIM (a modified subject or footer). ARC ([RFC 8617](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8617.html), Experimental) lets intermediaries record the results they saw; receivers decide whether to trust a given intermediary.

### Pulling headers apart in PowerShell

Header lines are folded: a line beginning with a space or tab continues the previous header. Unfold first, then parse:

```powershell
{{< include ../scripts/Get-MailHeader.ps1 >}}
```

```powershell
# Path, oldest hop first
Get-MailHeader -Path .\constructed-headers.eml |
	Where-Object Name -eq 'Received' |
	Sort-Object Order -Descending |
	Format-Table Order, Value -Wrap

Get-MailHeader -Path .\constructed-headers.eml |
	Where-Object Name -in 'Return-Path', 'From', 'Reply-To', 'Authentication-Results'
```

## SPF

**What SPF checks:** is the connecting IP allowed to send mail for the **envelope** domain? [RFC 7208](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208.html) evaluates the `MAIL FROM` domain, or the `HELO`/`EHLO` name when `MAIL FROM` is empty (bounces). It never looks at the `From` header.

```text
example.org.  TXT  "v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.0/24 include:_spf.esp.example -all"
```

| Mechanism | Matches when the IP… |
| --- | --- |
| `ip4:`, `ip6:` | is in the address or range |
| `a`, `mx` | is an A/AAAA address of the domain, or of its MX hosts |
| `include:` | passes the SPF policy of another domain |
| `exists:` | makes a constructed name resolve (advanced) |
| `all` | always; used last |
| `ptr` | reverse DNS matches; "SHOULD NOT" be used |

Each mechanism takes a qualifier: `+` pass (default), `-` fail, `~` softfail, `?` neutral. Results are `pass`, `fail`, `softfail`, `neutral`, `none`, `temperror` and `permerror`.

**Limits that cause real outages:** at most **10** mechanisms and modifiers that need DNS lookups (`include`, `a`, `mx`, `ptr`, `exists`, `redirect`) per evaluation, counting nested includes, and at most 2 lookups that return nothing (RFC 7208 §4.6.4). Exceeding them is a `permerror`, which DMARC treats as not passing. Only one SPF record per name is allowed; two is also a `permerror`.

**SPF pass does not necessarily mean DMARC pass.** It passes for the envelope domain. If that is a provider's bounce domain, SPF is not aligned with the `From` domain.

## DKIM

**What DKIM signs and verifies:** a signature over chosen header fields and the body, made with the signing domain's private key. The receiver fetches the public key from DNS and verifies. [RFC 6376](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376.html).

```text
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=relaxed/relaxed; d=example.org;
	s=esp2026; t=1792177329; h=from:to:subject:date:message-id;
	bh=47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=; b=Qx3fK9aL...

esp2026._domainkey.example.org.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqh..."
```

| Tag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `d=` | Signing domain: the identity DKIM authenticates, and what DMARC compares |
| `s=` | Selector: the key is at `<s>._domainkey.<d>` |
| `a=` | Algorithm, `rsa-sha256` or `ed25519-sha256` |
| `h=` | Header fields covered; `from` is required |
| `bh=` | Hash of the canonicalized body |
| `b=` | The signature |
| `c=` | Canonicalization for header/body, `simple` or `relaxed`: how tolerant it is of whitespace changes |
| `t=`, `x=` | Signature time and optional expiry |
| `l=` | Body length signed; anything after it is unsigned, so avoid it |

The `d=` domain does not have to match the `From` domain; DKIM only says "this domain took responsibility for this message." DMARC is what requires a match. An empty `p=` in the key record means the key was revoked.

## DMARC

DMARC ([RFC 9989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9989.html), May 2026) ties SPF and DKIM to the domain the user sees.

1. **Start with the domain in the message `From` header.** Look up `_dmarc.<that domain>`, walking up toward the organizational domain if there is no record.
2. **A message passes DMARC if SPF or DKIM passes *and* is aligned** with that domain. One is enough.
3. **Alignment.** *Strict* (`s`): the domains are identical. *Relaxed* (`r`, the default): they share an organizational domain, so `mail.example.org` aligns with `example.org`.
4. **Policy and reporting.** If DMARC fails, the domain owner's policy asks receivers to do nothing (`none`), treat it as suspicious (`quarantine`) or `reject` it, and where to send reports.

```text
_dmarc.example.org.  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.org"
```

### DMARC tags (RFC 9989 §4.7)

| Tag | Meaning | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `v` | Version; must be first | `DMARC1` | required |
| `p` | Policy for the domain | `none`, `quarantine`, `reject` | `none` if absent |
| `sp` | Policy for existing subdomains | as `p` | `p` |
| `np` | Policy for **non-existent** subdomains | as `p` | `sp`, then `p` |
| `adkim` | DKIM alignment | `r`, `s` | `r` |
| `aspf` | SPF alignment | `r`, `s` | `r` |
| `t` | Test mode: asks receivers not to apply the policy | `y`, `n` | `n` |
| `rua` | Aggregate report destinations | URIs | none |
| `ruf` | Failure report destinations | URIs | none |
| `fo` | Which failures generate failure reports | `0`, `1`, `d`, `s` | `0` |
| `psd` | Whether this is a public suffix domain | `y`, `n`, `u` | `u` |

### Work through email headers

These three exercises are from [learndmarc.com](https://www.learndmarc.com/), which builds and sends a test message and shows each step. Transcripts are reproduced as text. For each one, identify the sender identities, the SPF and DKIM results, and whether the message passes DMARC, and why.

#### Example 1

```smtp
. 220 smtp.learndmarc.com ESMTP Postfix
> HELO red.secondary.com
. 250 smtp.learndmarc.com Hello red.secondary.com <153.112.107.49>
> MAIL FROM: <gina@red.secondary.com>
. 250 Ok
> RCPT TO: <someone@yahoo.com>
> DATA
> From: "Gina" <gina@blue.secondary.com>
> DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=primary.com; s=selector; (DKIM Auth Result: PASS)
> Subject: Who reads the subject anyway?

Policies:
DMARC policy _dmarc.blue.secondary.com: "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; t=y;"
SPF policy red.secondary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:182.107.92.190 -all"
SPF policy blue.secondary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:24.121.50.128 ~all"
```

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**DMARC fails, the message will NOT be treated as suspicious.**

- Domain part `red.secondary.com` from the RFC5321.MailFrom address (MAIL FROM:) is used to retrieve the SPF policy.
- Domain part `blue.secondary.com` from the RFC5322.From address (From:) is used to check DMARC alignment.
- The message is signed with a DKIM signature and passed validation.
- SPF failed because source IP address 153.112.107.49 is NOT allowed to send on behalf of `red.secondary.com`.
- Having `t=y` in a DMARC policy signals that the Domain Owner is in test mode and requests that mail receivers not apply the stated handling policies (p, sp, or np) to messages that fail validation checks.
- The DMARC alignment policy is 'relaxed'. This is because the 'aspf' and 'adkim' elements were not specified or had an 'r' value. This means that only the organizational domains have to be in alignment.
- DKIM passed validation but there is NO alignment (`primary.com` != `secondary.com`).
- DMARC failed because neither SPF or DKIM passed validation and have alignment.

*Note:* had SPF passed, `red.secondary.com` would have aligned with `blue.secondary.com` under relaxed alignment: both have the organizational domain `secondary.com`.
</details>

#### Example 2

```smtp
. 220 smtp.learndmarc.com ESMTP Postfix
> HELO red.primary.com
. 250 smtp.learndmarc.com Hello red.primary.com <97.196.174.88>
> MAIL FROM: <terry@red.primary.com>
. 250 Ok
> RCPT TO: <someone@hotmail.com>
> DATA
> From: "Terry" <terry@blue.primary.com>
> DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=secondary.com; s=selector; (DKIM Auth Result: FAIL)
> Subject: I'll let myself out

Policies:
DMARC policy _dmarc.blue.primary.com: "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; adkim=s; aspf=s;"
SPF policy red.primary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:95.129.128.101 ~all"
SPF policy blue.primary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:44.62.173.139 ~all"
```

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**DMARC fails, the message will be quarantined.**

- Domain part `red.primary.com` from the RFC5321.MailFrom address (MAIL FROM:) is used to retrieve the SPF policy.
- Domain part `blue.primary.com` from the RFC5322.From address (From:) is used to check DMARC alignment.
- The message is signed with a DKIM signature but failed validation (auth result 'fail'), the message has been altered.
- SPF failed because source IP address 97.196.174.88 is NOT allowed to send on behalf of `red.primary.com`.
- The DMARC alignment policy is 'strict'. The 'aspf' and 'adkim' elements have an 's' value. This means that both domain and subdomain need to be an exact match.
- DMARC failed because neither SPF or DKIM passed validation and have alignment.
- DMARC failed and the policy is set to 'quarantine' so the requested action is to quarantine the message.

*Note:* the SPF record ends in `~all`, so learndmarc's "failed" is strictly an SPF **softfail**. For DMARC the distinction does not matter: only `pass` counts.
</details>

#### Example 3

```smtp
. 220 smtp.learndmarc.com ESMTP Postfix
> HELO blue.secondary.com
. 250 smtp.learndmarc.com Hello blue.secondary.com <156.157.23.197>
> MAIL FROM: <ray@blue.secondary.com>
. 250 Ok
> RCPT TO: <someone@gmail.com>
> DATA
> From: "Ray" <ray@red.primary.com>
> DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=blue.primary.com; s=selector; (DKIM Auth Result: PASS)
> Subject: DMARC test

Policies:
DMARC policy _dmarc.red.primary.com: "v=DMARC1; p=none; adkim=s; aspf=s;"
SPF policy blue.secondary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:62.165.120.61 ~all"
SPF policy red.primary.com: "v=spf1 ip4:156.157.23.197 -all"
```

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**DMARC fails, the message will NOT be treated as suspicious.**

- Domain part `blue.secondary.com` from the RFC5321.MailFrom address (MAIL FROM:) is used to retrieve the SPF policy.
- Domain part `red.primary.com` from the RFC5322.From address (From:) is used to check DMARC alignment.
- The message is signed with a DKIM signature and passed validation.
- SPF failed because source IP address 156.157.23.197 is NOT allowed to send on behalf of `blue.secondary.com`.
- The DMARC alignment policy is 'strict'. The 'aspf' and 'adkim' elements have an 's' value. This means that both domain and subdomain need to be an exact match.
- DKIM passed validation but there is NO alignment (`blue.primary.com` != `red.primary.com`).
- DMARC failed because neither SPF or DKIM passed validation and have alignment.
- DMARC failed but the policy is set to 'none' so no action will be taken.

*Notes:* the sending IP **is** listed in `red.primary.com`'s SPF record, which is a trap: SPF is evaluated for the `MAIL FROM` domain, not the `From` domain. And under relaxed alignment, the DKIM signature from `blue.primary.com` would have aligned with `red.primary.com`.
</details>

The answers above are learndmarc's explanations; the notes are additions.

## DNS records: lookups and troubleshooting

```powershell
Resolve-DnsName -Name example.org -Type MX
Resolve-DnsName -Name example.org -Type TXT | Where-Object { $_.Strings -match '^v=spf1' }
Resolve-DnsName -Name esp2026._domainkey.example.org -Type TXT
Resolve-DnsName -Name _dmarc.example.org -Type TXT
Resolve-DnsName -Name _mta-sts.example.org -Type TXT
Resolve-DnsName -Name _smtp._tls.example.org -Type TXT
```

```bash
dig +short MX example.org
dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.org
nslookup -type=txt _dmarc.example.org
```

Common problems:

| Symptom | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| SPF `permerror` | Two SPF records, a syntax error, or more than 10 DNS-lookup mechanisms after nested includes |
| SPF passes, DMARC fails | The envelope domain is the provider's, so SPF is not aligned; set up DKIM with your domain as `d=`, or a custom return-path domain |
| DKIM `fail` for one sender only | Wrong selector published, key rotated without DNS update, or a gateway that modifies messages after signing |
| DKIM passes, DMARC fails | The provider signs with its own domain; configure signing with your domain |
| Legitimate mail quarantined after moving to `p=quarantine` | A sender that was never inventoried; the aggregate reports would have shown it |
| Forwarded mail fails | Forwarding breaks SPF; DKIM survives only if the forwarder does not modify the message |

Look up the DKIM selector from a real message's `DKIM-Signature` (`s=`), not by guessing.

## DMARC reporting and the 2026 RFCs

### Aggregate reports (RFC 9990)

Receivers send daily-ish XML summaries to the `rua` address: for each sending IP, how many messages, the SPF and DKIM results, whether each aligned, and the disposition applied. [RFC 9990](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9990.html) defines the format. Reports are usually gzip-compressed attachments. This is how you find every service sending as your domain before you move from `p=none` to enforcement.

**Sending reports to another domain** (a vendor or a CRT-run mailbox) requires the destination to agree. For `_dmarc.example.org` with `rua=mailto:reports@dmarc.vendor.example`, receivers check for:

```text
example.org._report._dmarc.dmarc.vendor.example.  TXT  "v=DMARC1"
```

Without it they ignore that `rua` URI. This stops a domain from flooding a victim with reports.

### Failure reports (RFC 9991)

Per-message reports to the `ruf` address, controlled by `fo`. [RFC 9991](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9991.html) warns they can contain full headers and content, including personal information; many large receivers do not send them. Aggregate reports are the recommended default.

### What changed from RFC 7489

RFC 9989 obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091 and moves DMARC to the Standards Track (Appendix C):

| Change | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| `pct` removed | Partial enforcement by percentage is gone; `t=y` replaces part of its function |
| `t` added | Test mode: request that receivers not apply the policy |
| `np` added | Policy for non-existent subdomains (from RFC 9091) |
| `psd` added | Flags public suffix domains |
| `rf`, `ri` removed | Report format and interval tags |
| Organizational domain | Found by a **DNS tree walk** of `_dmarc` records (at most 8 queries) instead of the Public Suffix List |
| Reporting split out | Aggregate reporting is RFC 9990, failure reporting RFC 9991 |
| Terminology | "Domain Owner Assessment Policy," "Enforcement," "Monitoring Mode"; "Report Receiver" became "Report Consumer" |

Existing `v=DMARC1` records keep working; unknown tags are ignored, so a leftover `pct=` does no harm but no longer does anything for receivers that follow RFC 9989.

## Other email security mechanisms

### MTA-STS and TLS reporting

SMTP between servers uses opportunistic STARTTLS: an attacker on the path can strip it, and senders do not validate certificates by default. **MTA-STS** ([RFC 8461](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461.html)) lets a domain publish that its MX hosts support TLS with valid certificates, and that senders should refuse to deliver otherwise.

```text
_mta-sts.example.org.  TXT  "v=STSv1; id=20261016T000000;"
```

The policy is served over HTTPS at `https://mta-sts.example.org/.well-known/mta-sts.txt`:

```text
version: STSv1
mode: enforce
mx: mail.example.org
max_age: 604800
```

Start with `mode: testing`, and change `id` whenever the policy changes so senders refetch it.

**TLS-RPT** ([RFC 8460](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8460.html)) asks senders to report TLS negotiation failures, which is how you find out MTA-STS (or an expired MX certificate) is blocking mail:

```text
_smtp._tls.example.org.  TXT  "v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:tlsrpt@example.org"
```

### Sender ID (historical)

Microsoft's Sender ID (RFC 4406) checked a "purported responsible address" taken from the message headers rather than the envelope, and reused `v=spf2.0` records. The IETF experiment was concluded in [RFC 6686](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6686.html) (2012), which found SPF in wide use and Sender ID not. If you find `spf2.0/pra` records, they are leftovers.
